mechanism.rule: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Commercial Refrigerators, Freezers, and Refrigerator-Freezers (DOE final rule, RIN 1904-AD82, Docket EERE-2017-BT-STD-0007, 10 CFR part 431)
mechanism.agency: Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy, Department of Energy
mechanism.required: <cite index="31-2">DOE adopted new and amended energy conservation standards for commercial refrigeration equipment (CRE).</cite> <cite index="13-1">Manufacturers had to comply with the new and amended standards on and after January 22, 2029.</cite> The standards bind manufacturers of CRE. The costs and savings fall on the businesses that buy and run the equipment. DOE adopted trial standard level (TSL) 3. <cite index="10-3,10-9">On March 7, 2025, DOE delayed the effective date from March 24, 2025 to May 20, 2025 (90 FR 11466). The compliance date stayed January 22, 2029.</cite> The resolution did not amend the standards. It disapproved the rule, so that <cite index="8-3,8-5">the rule (90 FR 7464, published January 21, 2025) has no force or effect.</cite>
mechanism.benefits: DOE's own figures from the final rule (30-year analysis period, equipment shipped 2029–2058, 2023 dollars). (1) Consumer benefit: <cite index="59-2">the cumulative net present value of total consumer benefits is $1.32 billion at a 7% discount rate and $3.43 billion at 3%.</cite> (2) Health benefit: <cite index="59-6">the monetized value of reduced SO2 and NOx emissions at TSL 3 is $0.86 billion at 7% and $2.19 billion at 3%.</cite> (3) Energy savings: <cite index="63-1,63-2,63-3">primary energy savings over 2029–2058 are 1.11 quads, about 6.5% of the energy use of this equipment.</cite> (4) Emissions: <cite index="68-6">cumulative reductions of 19.7 million metric tons of CO2, 6.0 thousand tons of SO2 and 36.9 thousand tons of NOx.</cite> (5) Purchasers: <cite index="63-9">about 91% of affected CRE purchasers would see a net benefit or not be affected at TSL 3.</cite> (6) Net benefits: <cite index="58-7">including the manufacturer loss, annualized net benefits would be $537–540 million at a 3% discount rate and $444–447 million at 7%.</cite>
mechanism.costs: DOE's own figures from the same analysis. (1) Manufacturers: <cite index="63-5">DOE estimated industry net present value (INPV) without new standards at $3,022.3 million (2023$).</cite> <cite index="59-7">At TSL 3 the projected INPV change was a decrease of $78.7 million to $51.3 million, or 2.6% to 1.7%.</cite> A different DOE-hosted copy of the rule gives the low end of the range as about $77.8 million. (2) Purchasers: the NPV figures above are net of higher purchase and installation costs. Because about 91% of purchasers would see a net benefit or be unaffected, roughly 9% would have had a net cost. A garbled excerpt of the rule suggests payback periods of <cite index="30-10">0.9 to 7.0 years across equipment classes.</cite> (3) I did not retrieve DOE's annualized incremental equipment cost line, so it is not stated here. Official dispute of DOE's estimates: I found no CBO, GAO or court finding disputing them. GAO's major-rule report covers only the rule's content and dates.
mechanism.agency_reasons: <cite index="13-3">DOE determined that the new and amended standards would result in significant energy conservation and are technologically feasible and economically justified.</cite> <cite index="68-5">EPCA requires DOE to periodically review existing standards to see whether more-stringent standards would be technologically feasible, economically justified and save significant energy.</cite>
mechanism.sponsor_reasons: Rep. Craig Goldman (R-TX), the sponsor, said the resolution <cite index="39-8,39-9">repeals the previous administration's burdensome regulations on commercial refrigerators and freezers and blocks regulations that would have increased the cost of living.</cite> His office said <cite index="43-4">DOE estimated the standards would impose an $8 billion burden on small businesses and consumers.</cite> I could not verify that $8 billion figure in the DOE rule text I retrieved. House Energy and Commerce Chairmen Guthrie and Latta said the rule was <cite index="46-4">needless regulation raising prices for businesses and families while failing to provide cost savings or increasing food safety.</cite> The Energy and Commerce release also said <cite index="46-11">DOE itself estimated that at least one standard would have a payback period of more than 90 years.</cite> I could not verify that figure either. Rep. Goldman's op-ed argued the rule <cite index="41-3,41-4">fails the legal requirement that standards be technologically feasible and economically justified.</cite>
mechanism.status: Became law. <cite index="2-5">Public Law 119-9, May 9, 2025 (139 Stat. 52).</cite> Congress.gov records the House vote of March 27, 2025 (214-193) and the Senate passage vote (52-45). <cite index="53-7,53-8">President Trump signed the resolution on May 9, 2025, so the rule has no force or effect.</cite> <cite index="53-9">On May 20, 2025 DOE withdrew the rule and gave notice that its standards have no force or effect (90 FR 21392).</cite> The rule is void.

outcomes.claim: After the resolution became law, DOE withdrew the January 2025 final rule from the Federal Register. The amended CRE standards, with their January 22, 2029 compliance date, never took legal effect. DOE's regulatory agenda entry records the same sequence: the resolution was signed May 9, 2025 and the rule was withdrawn because it no longer has force or effect.
outcomes.counterpoint: This records the legal status only. It is not a measured effect on prices, energy use or businesses. A secondary source says covered CRE remains subject to the earlier federal standards and testing and certification requirements. I did not verify that against a primary document.

outcomes.claim: Benefits forgone, per DOE's pre-vote estimate. Over 2029–2058 shipments the standards were projected to deliver consumer net present value of $1.32 billion (7% discount rate) to $3.43 billion (3%), plus health benefits of $0.86–2.19 billion. They were also projected to save 1.11 quads of primary energy and cut CO2 by 19.7 million metric tons. About 91% of affected purchasers would see a net benefit or not be affected. This is a forecast, not a measured outcome. Whether these savings are in fact forgone depends on what purchasers and manufacturers do without the rule.

source.title: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Commercial Refrigerators, Freezers, and Refrigerator-Freezers (final rule)

outcomes.counterpoint: Sponsors disputed the rule's economics. They called it costly and not economically justified, and claimed a DOE-estimated $8 billion burden and a payback of more than 90 years for at least one standard. I could not confirm either figure in the DOE rule text I retrieved. DOE's published consumer NPV is positive at both discount rates. A CRS report notes that revoking a standard may have no energy-savings impact if consumers and firms keep buying the same mix of equipment.

outcomes.claim: Burden lifted, per DOE's pre-vote estimate. Manufacturers avoided a projected INPV loss of about $51.3–78.7 million (1.7–2.6% of a $3,022.3 million baseline, 2023$). About 9% of affected purchasers would have faced a net cost, since DOE estimated 91% would see a net benefit or not be affected. The compliance cost would have started in 2029.
outcomes.counterpoint: DOE judged the manufacturer loss small against the benefits. It said the consumer NPV at 7% was over 16 times the maximum INPV loss. Sponsors characterized the burden as far larger.

notes: (1) The figures come from search-result excerpts of the Federal Register and DOE documents. I did not open the full text or the Regulatory Impact Analysis / Technical Support Document, and some excerpts were garbled. Check the figures before publication, especially the 0.9–7.0 year payback range, the full-fuel-cycle energy savings at TSL 3, and DOE's annualized incremental equipment cost, which I did not retrieve. (2) DOE's INPV low-end figure appears as $78.7 million in one copy and about $77.8 million in another. (3) Third-party figures differ from DOE's consumer NPV of $1.32–3.43 billion. An advocacy group (Appliance Standards Awareness Project) cited nearly $4.6 billion in utility-bill savings over 30 years, as reported by the Washington Examiner. Nine state AGs cited $4.61 billion. I could not reconcile these with DOE's own numbers, so I did not use them as outcomes. (4) The $8 billion and 90-year payback claims are sponsor statements I could not trace to the DOE rule. (5) The effective date is given as the originally stated March 24, 2025. It was delayed to May 20, 2025, the day DOE withdrew the rule, and the rule never took effect. (6) The search results do not record what followed the withdrawal. I found no agency data, GAO or inspector general report, or peer-reviewed study on prices, energy use or business effects. The compliance date was 2029, so little could be measured yet. The search results do not show whether later DOE action restored or replaced the standards. This is a valid finding, not a gap to fill with inference. (7) The Congress.gov excerpt shows the Senate passage vote as 52-45. I did not retrieve the Senate roll-call pages for the motion to proceed (52-46) or the House roll call, so those counts are taken from the brief.
